The biggest risk is that the margin gains can't make up for slowing execution if order cover keeps shrinking. On top of that, working capital is stretched (negative FCF of ₹-826 cr in Q2FY26, debtor days around 113), and the Kurukshetra Expressway arbitration reversal could become a liability.

fundamental.thesis: Gland Pharma is a mid-cap injectables maker: it develops and manufactures injectable drugs for partners (B2B) and makes them to order for other drug companies (CDMO). fundamental.thesis: MRPL is a PSU mid-cap refinery (ONGC subsidiary) processing ~4.4 MMT/quarter of crude at Mangalore, operating in a policy-administered margin environment where GRMs, not crude price alone, drive earnings. H1FY27 revenue surged +67.6% YoY to ₹77,199 cr and PAT exploded +697.6% YoY to ₹2,846 cr (PAT margin 3.7%), a dramatic recovery from the near-zero-profit FY26 base (PAT margin 1.8%), with EBITDA margin expanding to 6.6% on strong throughput and higher product realisations — though a fire incident at the CHT unit on 30-Sep-2026 provisionally cost ₹118 cr and creates near-term operational uncertainty. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive refinery (per sector card guidance for PSU OMCs/refiners), MRPL trades at 5.97× EV/EBITDA versus a broad-market median of 23.3× — placing it at P3 in its peer universe — making it structurally cheap, though the sector card explicitly cautions this discount is 'policy-priced' (permanent policy risk, not a valuation error); trailing P/E of 14.5× sits at the upper end of the PSU OMC range (6–10× + yield), but the forward P/E collapses to 3.4×, implying the street is pricing in a very strong FY27 full-year earnings recovery. The key risk is that elevated crude at $97.97/bbl directly compresses refining marketing margins for OMC-adjacent refiners, estimate revisions are sharply negative (-9.6% 30d, -21.2% next-FY 90d) signalling analyst concern about GRM sustainability, and the CHT fire adds operational/insurance settlement uncertainty over the next 1–2 quarters.

For 9M CY26, revenue rose 20.3% YoY to ₹5,151 cr but PAT grew only 8.7% to ₹766 cr; backing out H1 (₹3,417 cr revenue, ₹590 cr PAT) implies the Sep-quarter revenue grew about 27% to roughly ₹1,734 cr while PAT fell about 22% to roughly ₹176 cr, so PAT margin dropped from 18.6% in the Jun quarter to about 10%, and the implied EBITDA margin of about 15% sits well below management's 21-24% target band. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardstick (not the PSU 'policy-priced' P/E-plus-yield framework), the stock trades at 17.7x trailing P/E and 11.9x EV/EBITDA, about 50% below the broad-market median (P18/P17), but trailing earnings include the stronger H1 and FY-EPS estimates were cut 4.9% over 30 days, so I grade it fair rather than cheap until margins stabilise. The biggest risk is that crude above $100 and a rupee at 95 per dollar keep raising base-oil costs faster than the company's low double-digit price hikes can pass them through, while weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.52x in H1) suggests working capital is soaking up the growth.

LT Foods is a midcap FMCG company that owns the Daawat rice brand, but its roughly 11% EBITDA margin is far from a typical premium staples profile. The Q2 FY27 numbers were filed on 2026-10-27 but were not extracted, so the latest usable quarter is Q1 FY27: revenue was Rs 3,161 cr (+26.0% YoY), with growth steady at about 24-26% across recent periods (the pre-computed 'decelerating' signal relies on a faulty Q2 FY26 row), while PAT was only Rs 183 cr (+9.0%) on a 5.8% margin, and gross margin fell from 34.4% in 9M FY26 to 32.6%. On trailing P/E of 21.5x, against an FMCG norm of 40-65x, and EV/EBITDA of 10.4x (P11 against a broad-market fallback, not close peers), the stock grades cheap, though the sector card warns that cheap FMCG often signals a structural problem, the 13.3x forward P/E implies earnings growth well above the current PAT trend, and the 7.5x P/B, 105% dividend yield and 28.49 debt/equity look unreliable and were given no weight. The main risk is that sales growth of 12% volume plus 11% price/mix keeps failing to reach profit, as in FY26 when revenue rose 26.1% but PAT only 2.2%, although cash conversion was sound at 1.46x CFO/PAT with FCF of Rs 551 cr.

fundamental.thesis: Maruti Suzuki is India's largest passenger-car maker and also a major exporter, with 1,379,378 units sold in H1 FY27, of which 232,855 were exports. H1 FY27 revenue rose 31.0% YoY to Rs 100,575 cr, with growth building from +12.7% in Q2 FY26 through +17.0% (9M) and +20.2% (FY26), but this was unprofitable growth: PAT fell 18.3% to Rs 5,767 cr after +7.3%, +4.0% and +1.0%, and PAT margin dropped from about 8.2-8.3% to 5.7%, while average selling price stayed roughly flat (Rs 729,370 vs Rs 729,189 in Q2 FY26), so growth is coming from volume rather than pricing; the Q2 FY27 row is blank, the yfinance Q2 revenue of Rs 40,432 cr does not reconcile with H1, and the FY26, 9M and Q2 FY26 rupee figures appear to be understated tenfold, which I inferred from volumes x selling price and corrected only in the margin and trend reads. Using the sector card's P/E yardstick for carmakers, cross-checked with EV/EBITDA, the stock is fair: 27.64x trailing P/E sits near the top of the 18-30x norm and matches the peer median of 27.1x (P60), and 18.32x EV/EBITDA is exactly at the peer median (P50), though my rough trailing-profit estimate of about Rs 13,150 cr implies closer to 31x, and the 20.82x forward P/E needs profit of about Rs 19,700 cr, roughly 50% higher. Being near the 52-week low (19.5% of range) helps risk/reward, but the biggest risk is that margins do not recover while crude rises, and sell-side upside looks overstated because the quoted +22% implies a price of about Rs 11,880, below the 52-week low, whereas the market cap implies about Rs 13,000, or roughly +11% to the mean target (the 107% dividend yield is also clearly a data error and was ignored).

fundamental.thesis: Wipro is India's fourth-largest IT services exporter and lags tier-1 peers on growth; the sector is in an AI-driven reset where legacy time-and-materials revenue is shrinking. H1FY27 revenue rose 9.8% YoY to ₹49,231 cr, a sharp pickup from near-flat FY26 (Q4FY26 at -0.2%), but PAT slipped 0.7% to ₹6,556 cr and PAT margin has compressed from 14.7% to 13.3% over the trend window. The revenue pickup probably owes part of its size to the Mindsprint acquisition and a weak rupee rather than real organic demand, and several trend rows look inconsistent, so the figures are unreliable. Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA as the yardsticks, Wipro is cheap: 15.6x P/E against a 22–30x sector band and a 24.7x peer median, and 10.5x EV/EBITDA, the lowest among its 8 peers. Cash conversion is strong (CFO/PAT 1.31x, net cash about ₹5,900 cr). The stock sits near its 52-week low. Sell-side coverage is heavily bearish (19 of 40 rate it sell) and estimates are drifting down, so the low multiple may be a value trap rather than mispricing.

Sun Pharma is India's largest drugmaker, with an 8.6% domestic market share (up 0.3pp), and a global generics and innovative-medicines business. Revenue growth improved from +10.1% in Q1 to +11.8% in Q2 (H1: Rs 31,499 cr, +11.0%), but it remains below +15.1% in Q3 FY26, and H1 PAT fell 9.5% to Rs 4,883 cr; implied Q2 PAT is about Rs 1,988 cr (roughly -36% YoY, 12.2% margin), hit by Organon deal and pricing-settlement charges, while adjusted H1 PAT rose only 2.2% and appears to be about Rs 6,251 cr after correcting a likely unit error, because the extracted Rs 62,515 cr and Rs 14,729 cr exceptional figures look to be in Rs million, and the trend table's pre-computed signals are also unreliable because they mix half-year and quarterly periods. Valuation is fair on trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA, the yardsticks used here: 37.4x P/E is within the 28-40x pharma range and at P54 among peers, while 24.2x EV/EBITDA is 13% above the peer median at P62, and earnings estimates are being cut (FY EPS -3.2% over 90 days) despite 28 of 33 analysts rating it a buy. The biggest risk is that the USD 14 bn Organon acquisition adds integration costs and likely debt just as US sales weaken (Q2 -8.2% on Lenalidomide erosion), while India formulations growth of 16.6% and a pre-deal net cash position of Rs 17,675 cr provide some cushion.

fundamental.thesis: ONGC is India's largest oil and gas producer, so its earnings rise with crude prices, but government policy can cap those gains. FY26 revenue fell 3.9% to Rs 132,508 cr and PAT fell 7.6% to Rs 32,894 cr, with the PAT margin down from 25.8% to 24.8%; on cumulative figures, the revenue decline narrowed from -9.4% in Q1 to -3.9% for the full year and the PAT decline from -10.2% to -7.6%, so the pre-computed 'decelerating' signal, which mixes period lengths, looks unreliable, and Q1 FY27 is missing from the trend table with Q2 FY27 results due at the 5 Nov board meeting. Using the sector card's P/E-plus-yield yardstick for PSU upstream names, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the 8.04x trailing P/E sits inside the 6-10x norm and is 12.8% below the 9.2x peer median, while EV/EBITDA of 4.56x is 24.9% below the peer median, so the grade is fair (policy-priced) rather than cheap, even with P/B at 0.9x and ROE at 12.7%; the yield leg could not be checked because the 699% dividend yield is clearly a data error, and the 42.55 debt/equity reading also looks like a percentage (about 0.43x) and needs verifying. The biggest risk is that $96 crude does not reach earnings if the government intervenes through windfall-style levies or gas pricing, and the stale filings mean the current earnings run-rate is unconfirmed.

Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, valuation is fair rather than cheap: 21.0x is 38% below the Industrials median of 34.0x (P24) and trailing P/E of 31.25x is at P12, but those peers are mostly richly priced electrical and defence names rather than port operators, and the stock sits at 95.6% of its 52-week range. fundamental.thesis: JSW Steel is a large Indian steelmaker that sold a record 7.46 MT in Q2FY27 (+13% YoY), with auto-sector sales up 36%. Revenue growth accelerated from +9.8% in Q1 to +20.6% (₹54,486 cr), and PAT rose 225.6% to ₹5,359 cr, though the YoY figures use a low, restructured base; PAT margin was flat at about 9.8-9.9%, the 'contracting' signal is distorted by FY26's ₹18,051 cr one-off gain, and EBITDA per tonne fell about 11% QoQ from ₹14,990 to ₹13,329 despite rising 24% YoY. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a steel cyclical, the stock is expensive: the reported 12.6x, or roughly 9x on my estimate using annualised Q2 EBITDA and net debt, is above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, and the 13.8x trailing P/E and 'cheap vs peers' verdict carry little weight because of the one-off gain and a peer set that includes paint and adhesive companies. The biggest risk is that steel spreads narrow from here, with the stock at 92% of its 52-week range and EBITDA per tonne already falling sequentially, leaving little room for error.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles is India's second-largest OEM and houses the Jaguar Land Rover luxury brand globally; post the CV demerger (effective Oct 2025) it is a pure-play on domestic EVs and JLR's BEV transition, with domestic EV mix rising to ~14.3% of volumes. Q1FY27 revenue recovered to +9.3% YoY (₹95,799 cr) after troughs of -25.8% in Q3FY26 — a genuine acceleration — but PAT collapsed -78.5% YoY to ₹859 cr as EBITDA margins contracted 130 bps YoY to 7.4%, driven by elevated JLR vehicle material expenses, commodity/FX headwinds, and a 9.2% JLR wholesale volume decline from supplier fire and the Jaguar brand wind-down. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive OEM, TMPV trades at 7.09× vs the sector median of 18.3× (P0 — cheapest in peer group), and forward P/E of 7.15× vs peer median 20.8× — deeply cheap, but that discount reflects real distress: negative TTM ROE of -1.1%, extreme leverage (D/E 65.31), and 90-day EPS estimate cuts of -20.6%. The core risk is that JLR's four planned BEV launches fail to fill the Jaguar volume gap while high leverage leaves no cushion for further margin disappointment.

Coal India is India's dominant domestic coal producer, earning a largely domestic volume and e-auction-premium annuity, with cash generation as the main support (H1 FY27 CFO/PAT 2.21x, FCF Rs 26,270 cr). H1 FY27 revenue rose 13.8% YoY to Rs 90,434 cr and PAT rose 18.9% to Rs 15,397 cr, but offtake (+7.6%) was met by drawing down inventory while production fell 2%, and EBITDA margin slipped to about 29% from 32% in FY26; the pre-computed deceleration and margin signals are unreliable because they compare H1, full-year and nine-month periods and count H1 twice, and no standalone Q2 figures are available from filings. On the sector card's yardstick of P/E plus yield, backed by EV/EBITDA, valuation is fair and policy-priced rather than cheap: trailing P/E is 9.22x against a 6-10x norm, EV/EBITDA is 6.07x (P50 among peers), and forward P/E is 8.13x, though the stock is at 85% of its 52-week range, and the 466% dividend yield and 11.63 debt/equity readings look like data errors and were ignored. The biggest risk is that growth has relied on stock drawdown, not production, while estimates are drifting slightly lower (FY EPS -0.9% over 30 days), and the +12.6% consensus upside looks misstated because market cap and range position imply a price near Rs 470, above the Rs 459 mean target.

Valuation is fair on the auto card's P/E yardstick, cross-checked with EV/EBITDA because the Rs 25,126 cr revenue includes low-margin consolidation effects: trailing P/E of 26.6x is inside the 18-30x OEM range and 1.9% below the 27.1x peer median (P40), while EV/EBITDA of 19.8x is 8.1% above the peer median (P67) and the stock sits at 85% of its 52-week range, which limits upside despite FY EPS estimates rising 10.3% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that input-cost inflation of about 8% of revenue in H1, only about 60% recovered through pricing, continues into Q3 just as rupee support fades and rural demand weakens; some data also conflicts, including a stale-filing flag, a yfinance revenue mismatch and an implausible 145% dividend yield, so those items were not relied on.

fundamental.thesis: Ashok Leyland is India's second-largest commercial vehicle manufacturer (MHCV + LCV), with a dominant domestic franchise and Hinduja Group backing — a cyclical play on infrastructure-linked freight demand and government fleet renewal (Parivartan). Using P/B against ROE as the lender yardstick, the stock looks cheap at 3.04x book for about 30% ROE: P/B is in line with the peer median (P44), trailing P/E of 11.2x is 44% below peers (P22), forward P/E is 8.6x and FY EPS estimates are up 4.4% over 90 days, but this assumes today's ROE lasts, and I discount it because a lower ROE would make the multiple closer to fair. fundamental.thesis: Central Bank of India is a mid-sized public-sector lender whose recent story has been cleaning up bad loans: gross NPA fell from 3.02% (H1 FY26) to 2.67% (FY26), net NPA is about 0.5%, and provision coverage is very high at about 96%. Loan growth has been strong at 17.7–20.7% YoY. FY26 PAT was ₹4,531 cr, up 15.0%, and Q3FY26 PAT was ₹378 cr, up 33.5% in the extracted series. However, margin health is weakening: NIM fell from 3.12% to 2.69%, ROA slipped from 1.07% to 0.92%, and capital adequacy fell from 17.34% to 16.13% as fast lending used up capital. Because this is a lender, I graded valuation on P/B and ROE, not P/E. At 0.77x book with an 11.9% ROE (trailing P/E 6.6x against a 12–18x bank range, P1 on P/B in the broad-market peer set), the stock looks cheap, sits at 33% of its 52-week range, and the market seems to be pricing in an ROE just below the 12% mark. The Q2FY27/H1FY27 results filed on 2026-10-17 have not been read, so all figures here are stale. That, plus NIM compression, an underweight Financials tilt and a risk-off macro backdrop, keeps conviction moderate.

Petronet LNG imports and regasifies LNG through its terminals, and its earnings depend mainly on volumes and tariffs rather than LNG prices. Only H1 FY27 figures are available, so no quarterly trend can be established: revenue fell 44.3% YoY to Rs 12,760 cr because of the Middle East force majeure and vessel suspensions, while PAT rose 43.1% to Rs 2,394 cr (18.8% margin), EBITDA margin widened from 13.2% to 30.4%, and CFO/PAT was a solid 1.25x. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock is fair at 6.11x, in line with the 6.1x sector median (P67), and its 10.31x trailing P/E sits within the 8-14x sector range; yfinance's 372% dividend yield and 10.51 debt/equity look like unit errors (about 3.7% and 0.11x), and the +5.5% consensus upside conflicts with the roughly Rs 269 price implied by the 52-week position. The biggest risk is that profit rose despite the revenue collapse, so its durability is unproven while the vessel owners' Rs 625 cr arbitration claims and Rs 408 cr of gross Use-or-Pay dues remain unresolved.

The biggest risk is that growth slows as the easy base fades while the valuation still assumes a strong recovery, and next-year EPS estimates have already been cut 8.8% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Go Digit General Insurance is a tech-first non-life insurer with motor (55% of gross premium) as its core segment, competing against established incumbents in a scale-driven, commoditising market. Q1FY27 delivered a sharp deterioration: gross premium written fell 8.4% YoY to ₹2,731 cr and PAT collapsed 37.5% YoY to ₹86 cr, as the combined ratio worsened to 112.3% (from 108.6% a year ago) on rising incurred claims (73.3% vs 70.3%) and an expense management ratio that breached IRDAI regulatory limits at 39% vs 35% prior year — the revenue trend has decelerated from +6.4% to -8.4% over three comparable periods and PAT margin compressed from 7.4% to 3.2% over the same window. Using P/B + ROE as the appropriate yardstick for an insurer (sector card), at P/B of 4.95× against a FY26 ROE of 17.7% that is clearly trending down in FY27, the stock is expensive — the justified P/B on a declining ROE trajectory sits well below 4× — and the trailing P/E of 47× (above the 18–28× NBFC benchmark) merely confirms the premium; the forward P/E of 28× prices in a full earnings recovery that the current underwriting data does not yet support. The biggest risk is that the combined ratio remains structurally above 100% — driven by Motor TP claims elevated post the Supreme Court's Shishupal judgment — while management's underwriting tightening (deliberate pullback from unprofitable premiums) continues to compress both the top line and market share.

Q3FY26 (latest extracted official data) showed revenue of ₹3,427 cr (+40.4% YoY) and PAT of ₹464 cr (+1,040% YoY off a severely depressed Q3FY25 base of ₹82 cr), with PAT margin expanding from 6.4% (Q3FY25) to 13.5% (Q3FY26) and GNPA improving from 2.4% to 1.6% — but Q2FY27 results filed October 15 remain unextracted, leaving a ~9-month data gap that materially limits current visibility. The biggest fundamental risk is governance: the re-designation of co-founder R Venkataraman from Joint MD to Non-Executive Director on October 15 is a leadership change at a sensitive recovery juncture, compounded by a declining Provision Coverage Ratio (114% in Q3FY25 to 63% in H1FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT −7.34×), all of which limit conviction despite the appealing valuation.

fundamental.thesis: Niva Bupa is a standalone health insurer with 11.1% of the retail health market, 26 million lives covered and retail health premiums up 47% YoY, so it is one of the fastest-growing players in an under-insured market. In Q1FY27, gross written premium rose 32.0% YoY to ₹2,150 cr and PAT rose 93% to ₹138 cr (6.4% margin, up from a loss of ₹9 cr in Q3FY26 and 2.1% for FY26). But the trend table mixes periods and bases (Q3FY26 revenue of ₹223 cr doesn't fit the other rows), and the combined ratio is 100.2%, so underwriting only breaks even and profit depends on investment income. A trailing P/E of 75× isn't meaningful for a business whose earnings are still ramping. On my yardstick for an insurer, P/B against ROE, 3.84× book for a 12.1% ROE is full, while the 23.5× forward P/E sits at the peer median (P51) and EV/EBITDA at P54, so I grade it fair: growth is priced in, not mispriced. The biggest risk is claims inflation pushing the combined ratio above 100%, with Q2FY27 results due within days; the 17-Oct exit of non-executive director Roger Davis is a minor governance item to watch.

Choice International is a mid-cap financial services group that earns most of its revenue from broking and also runs advisory, wealth and NBFC businesses, with 13.78 lakh demat accounts and ₹66,300 Cr of client assets. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 35.9% YoY to ₹373 Cr, up from about +32-34% in Q1 (the two Q1 records differ), but PAT growth slowed from +26.4% to +23.0% to ₹70 Cr; the PAT margin fell from 19.88% to 18.33% YoY as employee costs rose 45% and finance costs 49%, so I disregard the table's 'expanding' margin signal, which appears to misread the order of the periods. On my main yardstick of P/B against ROE, 8.37x book for a 16.2% ROE looks expensive, and the 63.1x trailing P/E is well above the 18-28x NBFC range and at P80 of a broad-market peer set rather than close peers, while the 47.1x forward P/E already prices in strong growth and the mid-range 52-week position (47.6%) offers no clear entry advantage. The biggest risk is that this premium multiple rests on market-linked broking and IPO earnings in a risk-off market, while growth is becoming more costly and the ₹900 Cr NH Investment preference share deal could dilute the parent's stake in its main subsidiary once converted.

Subtracting Q1 from H1 implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 3,243 cr, up 16.2% YoY (slowing from +28.3% in Q1), and PAT of about Rs 250 cr, a 7.7% margin against 12.0% in Q1; PAT fell about 21% against the reported Rs 318 cr, though it looks roughly flat if the prior-year land-sale gain sits in that quarter, and the reported H1 PAT drop of 62.9% mostly reflects the earlier railway business sale, with continuing PAT up only 2.2%. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardsticks because order-book measures do not fit this business, valuation looks fair rather than cheap at 16.3x EV/EBITDA and 22.6x trailing P/E: it is below the 28-45x Industrials range but inside the 18-28x Auto range that better suits a tractor maker, the P28-P30 peer ranks are against the broad market rather than close peers, and the 19.8x forward P/E rests on FY estimates already cut 11.6%. The main risk is that revenue growth is not reaching profit or cash, with agri EBIT margin down 340 bps to 9.3%, H1 operating cash flow at -Rs 107 cr on an inventory and receivables build, and management's margin recovery from Q4 dependent on stable commodity costs while crude is rising; the Rs 698 cr net cash cushions this, but the 1.31 debt/equity reading conflicts with it, and the 117% dividend yield, H1 EBITDA margin comparisons and +30.8% consensus upside also look unreliable, so none of them were relied on.

Q1FY27 revenue grew just +0.8% YoY (₹6,795 cr), a sharp deceleration from the +27–33% range seen across FY26 and H1FY26, but EBITDA surged 23.3% YoY to ₹3,190 cr on 854 bps of margin expansion to 46.9%, and PAT held at ₹1,976 cr (+0.4% YoY, 29.1% margin) — the revenue line has stalled while operational leverage has sharply improved. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple per sector card guidance for capital-intensive commodity names, NMDC trades at 7.81×, within the 5–8× mid-cycle commodity range and at P6 (cheapest 6%) vs 473 broader-market peers; trailing P/E of 10.45× sits below the 12–22× Materials sector lower bound — graded cheap, though the EV/EBITDA at the top of the mid-cycle range limits the cheapness margin. The dominant overhang is the ₹15,785.72 cr Karnataka Mineral Rights Tax contingent liability (≈20% of market cap), awaiting Presidential assent, combined with ₹11+ cr of stressed receivables from demerged NSL and government-owned RINL that depressed CFO/PAT cash conversion to 0.66× in FY26.

Gravita India recycles lead, copper, aluminium and plastics, with lead still 62% of H1 revenue and the main profit driver at a 10.6% margin, while the copper segment added through the RMIL acquisition is 27% of revenue at only a 3.0% margin. Q2FY27 revenue rose 38.0% to Rs 1,427 cr, but this growth is flattered by the March 2026 RMIL deal (the organic split is not disclosed in the data provided); PAT growth slowed from +14.3% in Q1 to +6.0% at Rs 102 cr, EBITDA margin fell from 16.5% in H1FY26 to 10.0%, and CFO/PAT was -0.33x in H1FY27 with FCF of Rs -210 cr. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-intensive metals business, 24.0x looks expensive against the sector card's 5-8x for cyclical materials and the 33.2x trailing P/E is above the 12-22x Materials range, though recycling is not a direct match for those norms and the P52 peer rank is only a broad-market fallback; the 21.7x forward P/E needs strong earnings growth while FY estimates are being cut (-1.8% and next-FY -3.0% over 90 days) despite 10 of 10 buy ratings, and several feed values look unreliable, so I ignored the 64% dividend yield and the yfinance revenue of Rs 1,167 cr, read Debt/Equity of 29.93 as a probable 0.30x, and estimate the Rs 1,920 mean target at about +11-13% (price about Rs 1,700-1,725 from market cap and 52-week position) rather than +35.5%. The biggest risk is that acquired low-margin copper revenue keeps diluting margins while working capital absorbs cash, leaving little room at this valuation for further estimate cuts.

fundamental.thesis: UPL is India's largest global agrochemical company, operating crop protection (UPL Corp), seeds (Advanta), and post-harvest segments across 130+ countries — a capital-intensive, leveraged cyclical recovering from a multi-year agrochem destocking cycle. Revenue has accelerated from a trough of +2% YoY in Q1FY26 to +10% YoY in Q1FY27 (₹10,181 cr consolidated); EBITDA grew 15% YoY to ₹1,500 cr with 180 bps contribution-margin expansion, and Q1FY27 PATMI was management's stated strongest in three years — a clear directional improvement from the -₹88 cr loss in Q1FY26, supported by broad-based platform growth (Advanta +26%, SUPERFORM +14%, UPL Corp +7%). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per sector card guidance), UPL at 7.86× sits at P6 vs. 473 broad-market peers (67% discount to the 23.3× median) and at the mid-cycle floor for specialty chemicals (5–8× range); forward P/E of 12.65× is 46% below trailing 27.34×, signalling substantial earnings recovery priced in — the stock grades cheap on the appropriate metric. The primary risk is the combination of very high financial leverage (D/E flagged as extreme), NWC deteriorating sharply to 110 days (+24 days YoY from inventory build and FX translation), and persistent China-led price competition in agrochemicals — all amplified by rising crude input costs, INR weakness expanding USD-denominated debt service costs, and an ongoing RISK_OFF macro regime with FII net selling.

Q1FY27 revenue grew +11.9% YoY to ₹5,349 cr — a meaningful deceleration from +15.0% in Q3FY26 — though PAT surged +28.8% YoY to ₹427 cr (margin 8.0% vs 7.0% a year ago), powered by lower tea input costs and gross-margin expansion from 40.1% to 42.7%; volume growth in the India business was ~13%, solid but to be weighed against the sector card's caution on >10% volume claims. At a trailing P/E of 60.51× — at the upper bound of the FMCG benchmark range of 40–60× and ranked P78 among broad-market peers — the stock screens as expensive even near its 52-week low; however, a forward P/E of 41.78× (31% below trailing) signals the market is pricing in a meaningful earnings step-up from acquisition integration and tea-cost tailwinds. The principal risk is sustained revenue growth deceleration toward sub-10% alongside a reported Debt/Equity of 12.16 (reflecting heavy acquisition financing), which leaves the stock highly exposed to multiple compression if earnings delivery disappoints or high-rate conditions pressure interest coverage.

fundamental.thesis: IKS (Inventurus Knowledge Solutions) provides AI-enabled clinical documentation and physician support services to US healthcare systems, occupying a niche but rapidly scaling position in healthcare administrative outsourcing. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue grew +20.7% YoY to ₹894 cr (vs ₹740 cr in Q1FY26) with PAT up +27.8% YoY to ₹194 cr; importantly, revenue growth has been remarkably stable at 20–21% across four consecutive periods — the trajectory signals show only a modest deceleration (+21.5% → +19.9% → +20.7%) — while PAT margin has mildly contracted from 23.1% (Q2FY26) to 21.7% (Q1FY27), a ~140bps compression that warrants watching but is not yet alarming given strong CFO/PAT conversion of 2.20×. At a trailing P/E of 39.84× the stock sits above the IT services sector median of 22–30×, but the forward P/E collapses to 25.71× (consistent with ~28% PAT growth), and peer analysis places IKS at P56–58 — broadly in line with the broad-market median — yielding a 'fair' valuation verdict; the P/B of 10.4× (P83 vs peers) is elevated but defensible for a capital-light, high-margin services compounder if growth sustains. The primary risk is a debt/equity ratio of 26.87 — structurally anomalous for a services business — combined with a recent senior management change (Sept 4 filing) that could signal disruption to the execution culture underpinning the growth narrative.

Q2 FY27 revenue was Rs 855 cr, with YoY growth slowing from +36.2% in Q2 FY26 to +20.6% in Q1 FY27 and +13.0% now, while PAT of Rs 104 cr rose only 1.8% as EBITDA margin slipped to 23.2% from 24.3% a year ago, although it improved from 22.3% last quarter; platform revenue also fell to Rs 133 cr from Rs 141 cr sequentially, despite 21 new customers and 8 large Destiny deals. On our main yardstick of trailing P/E, supported by EV/EBITDA, the stock is fair: 31.15x is just above the 22-30x IT range and 17.0x EV/EBITDA is only moderately below the broad-market median, while the 18.4x forward P/E relies on estimates that were cut 9.7% for this year and 12.7% for next year over the past 30 days, and the 53% dividend yield, 4.96 debt/equity and +51.6% target upside look like data errors and were ignored. The biggest risk is that AI spending keeps absorbing profit (management attributes over Rs 100 cr of LTM cost to AI investments, and LTM PBT is down 6.2%) while revenue growth continues to slow.

fundamental.thesis: NHPC is India's largest hydropower generator. Because this is a capital-intensive regulated business, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/B+ROE. On those measures the signals conflict: EV/EBITDA of 25.5x is rich for a utility, and a P/B of 1.85x for a ROE of only 9% is not cheap. On the other side, the forward P/E of 11.9x (bottom 14% of the market) and P/B in the bottom 16% suggest the market already expects the Subansiri Lower and Parbati-II earnings ramp, so overall I grade it fair. The biggest risk is weak cash conversion: free cash flow was -₹3,850 cr in FY26, CFO/PAT was 0.62x, and leverage is high (debt/equity about 1.13x). Earnings also depend on about ₹939 cr of provisional revenue that CERC has not yet approved, and Q2 results are due on 4 Nov 2026.

fundamental.thesis: Deepak Fertilisers is a mid-cap ammonia-chain business. Profitability has been shrinking through the year: PAT margin slid from 8.1% (H1) to 7.0% (9M) to 6.4% (full year), and EBITDA margin from 17.3% to 14.6%. The filing-extracted trend table has no Q1 FY27 revenue or PAT, and the unverified yfinance figure (PAT ₹490 cr on ₹1,886 cr revenue) looks like it may include a one-off. The biggest risks are a slow ramp-up at the new plants with debt high (debt/equity about 0.76) and free cash flow negative (−₹396 cr in H1 FY26), together with raw-material squeeze from the Middle East and a falling-margin trend.

fundamental.thesis: Swiggy is India's number-two food-delivery and quick-commerce (Instamart) platform, with a small but fast-growing out-of-home dining segment. Revenue keeps growing in the mid-30s: H1 FY27 rose 36.7% to ₹14,383 cr, and the implied Q2 is about ₹7,571 cr, up roughly 36% YoY, slower than FY26's +51.4%. The trend-table label 'accelerating' mixes half-year, full-year and quarterly periods and overstates the move. Losses are narrowing on a YoY basis: the H1 EBITDA loss fell to ₹997 cr from ₹1,606 cr and H1 net loss to ₹1,713 cr from ₹2,289 cr. Sequentially, however, the Q2 loss widened to about ₹922 cr from ₹791 cr in Q1. Food delivery is close to breakeven at a -7.65% margin, but Instamart still lost ₹1,415 cr at a -55.9% margin. Because P/E and EV/EBITDA are meaningless while the company is loss-making, I graded valuation on EV/sales plus unit-economics delivery, as the sector card prescribes for platforms. Price/sales of 2.89x (about 2.3x on annualised H1 revenue) and P/B of 3.35x (P37 vs the broad market) look fair, not stretched, for ~36% growth with improving margins. Sell-side estimates have been revised sharply upward (FY EPS +50.7% over 90 days), but there is no formal management guidance, and the main risk is that the Instamart cash burn in the quick-commerce price war delays group profitability.

fundamental.thesis: Urban Company is India's largest online platform for home services such as beauty, cleaning and repairs, and it also sells its own water purifiers and smart locks (Native), runs international operations and has a Saudi joint venture. It is now funding a heavily loss-making quick home-help business called InstaHelp. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹537 cr, up 41% YoY, faster than FY26's +36%. Orders rose 103% and Net Transaction Value (NTV, the total value of services booked) rose 39% to ₹1,432 cr. Profit went the other way: consolidated adjusted EBITDA was -₹144 cr, a -26.8% margin, against +6.8% for FY26. That is because InstaHelp lost ₹174 cr, which wiped out a core business that is profitable and improving (core EBITDA ₹30 cr, up 213% YoY; India consumer margin 3.5%, up 110 bps). Since the business is pre-profit, P/E means nothing here, so I graded valuation on price-to-sales and unit economics instead. At 12.3x sales and 8.6x book value (76th percentile of the broad market), the price is reasonable for 40% growth only if InstaHelp's losses keep shrinking. InstaHelp's loss per order did improve 19% from the previous quarter but is still ₹279. I rate valuation fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that the InstaHelp cash burn continues while the newly approved ₹2,500 cr capital raise dilutes shareholders, in a risk-off market that punishes high-multiple loss-makers.

fundamental.thesis: Zee Entertainment is India's second-largest broadcast media group (~50 TV channels plus the ZEE5 OTT platform), structurally pressured by the secular migration to streaming and left exposed after the Jiostar/Sony merger collapsed; it now carries substantial governance and legal overhangs that suppress any re-rating. FY26 annual revenue declined 1.9% YoY to ₹7,567 Cr while PAT collapsed 82.8% to ₹120 Cr, compressing PAT margin to 1.6% and EBITDA margin to a catastrophic 2.6% (from 13.4% in FY25) — the multi-quarter trajectory shows revenue decelerating and margins contracting across every available period with no stabilisation evident in filings. Forward P/E of 13.42× (P19 vs broad-market peers, -42% below median) and P/B of 0.9× (P2 vs peers, -80% below median) both screen as unambiguously cheap; EV/EBITDA of 23× looks deceptively at median but is computed on severely depressed EBITDA — on normalised 12-13% margins the implied EV/EBITDA would be sub-5×, confirming franchise-level cheapness if operational recovery is achievable. The single largest risk to the recovery thesis is the IDBI Bank insolvency petition (filed September 2025) seeking NCLT-admitted CIRP initiation, which if granted would be existential for the business regardless of underlying brand and content-IP value.

Ather Energy is a pure-play premium electric two-wheeler maker with 15.1% market share, down from 17.2% a year ago, and 15% of revenue comes from non-vehicle sources. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 62.8% YoY to Rs 1,464 cr on 42% higher volumes and 14.6% higher revenue per unit, compared with +53% in Q3FY26 and +66% for FY26, while PAT improved from a Rs 154 cr loss to a Rs 1.26 cr profit and EBITDA margin moved from -3.0% in Q3FY26 to 5.0%, although the missing Q1FY27 row and mixed annual and quarterly periods make the 'accelerating' signal unreliable. Valuation is expensive using the pre-profit yardstick of EV/sales proxied by P/S, growth delivery and unit economics rather than trailing P/E: P/S is 15.5x (about 11x annualised Q2 revenue), forward P/E is 374x, and the stock is near its 52-week high with the mean target about level with the price, though EV/EBITDA is not meaningful, no tight peer set is available, and the price inputs and 25.82 debt/equity figure look inconsistent or unclear and were given little weight. The biggest risk is that aluminium, copper and memory-chip cost inflation interrupts margin gains while share is falling, a concern supported by next-FY EPS estimates being cut 49% in 30 days even as all 12 analysts stay at buy.

fundamental.thesis: Balrampur Chini Mills is one of India's largest integrated sugar companies, with operations spanning sugar milling, ethanol distillation, and power co-generation — a commodity-linked agri-business with meaningful policy exposure (sugar MSP, ethanol blending mandates). The multi-quarter revenue trajectory shows deceleration (from +28.7% in Q2FY26 to +6.1% in Q1FY27), while PAT margins have contracted sharply to 2.7% in Q1FY27 from a prior-year 3.4%, with PAT declining -14.4% YoY to ₹44 cr despite modest revenue growth — this is a deteriorating fundamental picture. At trailing P/E of 38×, BALRAMCHIN trades at the lower bound of the FMCG sector benchmark (40–65×) and sits at P55 in the broad market — the forward P/E of 18.5× (a steep discount to trailing) signals the market is pricing in a meaningful earnings recovery, likely tied to ethanol blending expansion and improved sugar realisations; however, the -20.3% forward P/E discount to peers and P/B of 3.4× (below market median of 4.6×) together suggest fair-to-cheap valuation using EV/EBITDA (25×, slightly above peer median of 23.3×). The primary risk is that this is a sugar company masquerading as FMCG — earnings are seasonal, cyclically volatile, and heavily dependent on government-set cane prices, ethanol blending mandates, and export policy; high debt/equity of 76.6 combined with negative FY26 FCF of -₹349 cr and a suspicious dividend yield of 99% (likely a data artefact) warrants governance scrutiny before any position.

On the IT yardstick (P/E backed by EV/EBITDA), trailing P/E is 21.8x, just under the 22–30x IT range, with forward P/E at 18.2x and EV/EBITDA at 13.0x, so I grade it fair: the discount is marginal, and sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 6.1% over 90 days, so the forward multiple may be too flattering. Parry is a sugar, distillery and nutraceuticals business whose consolidated numbers are dominated by its farm-inputs subsidiary CIL (nutrient segment Rs 6,951 cr of about Rs 9,018 cr Q1 FY27 revenue), so it is closer to a fertiliser holding company than the FMCG name its sector tag suggests. Revenue growth slowed from +18.3% in Q3 FY26 to +3.4% in Q1 FY27, and PAT fell 42.5% YoY to Rs 142 cr, a 1.6% margin against 2.8% a year earlier, with EBITDA margin down from 10.3% to 8.7% and the standalone business loss-making (PAT of -Rs 89 cr). Using EV/EBITDA and P/B rather than the FMCG P/E norm, valuation is cheap at 5.96x EV/EBITDA and 1.53x book (P2 and P11 against a broad-market peer set, trailing P/E 29.06x), but consolidated EV/EBITDA is probably flattered by minority interests in the subsidiary, and the 10.1x forward P/E rests on thin coverage with estimates cut 30.2% in 90 days. The biggest risk is that the Q2 FY27 results due from the 13 November board meeting face a high base (Rs 424 cr PAT) while the refinery closure, weak distillery and sugar losses persist; some inputs also look unreliable, including refinery figures likely misstated in units, a D/E of 23.65 that may be a percentage, and a consensus upside of +69.8% that does not reconcile with the roughly Rs 756 price implied by the snapshot.

Q1 FY27 revenue was about ₹714 cr (+174.5% YoY) with PAT of ₹85 cr (+196.5%), and yfinance shows Q2 FY27 at about ₹1,091 cr revenue and ₹137 cr PAT. However, the extracted H1 FY27 figures (₹2,143 cr revenue, 19.7% PAT margin) do not reconcile with these quarters and come from an OCR-corrupted filing, so the exact Q2 growth rate and margin step-up are unverified; EBITDA margin also eased from 14.9% to 12.2–13.0% across FY26. Valuation is expensive on any yardstick: trailing P/E is 108.7x against an IT median of 22–30x, forward P/E is 60.7x and EV/EBITDA is 79.2x (I used EV/EBITDA as the primary measure for a hardware business), the stock ranks around P94–P96 against the broad market, and it sits at 74% of its 52-week range. Rising sell-side estimates (FY EPS +11.8% over 90 days) support momentum but leave little room for any slip in lumpy, order-driven revenue.

CESC is a West Bengal-regulated power utility with a coal mine and other power operations, and its earnings depend heavily on tariff orders and regulatory income. In FY26, revenue rose 9.2% to Rs 18,570 cr and PAT rose 12.6% to Rs 1,542 cr, but no reliable filing data is available after FY26, and the trend signals mix annual and part-year periods, so I cannot confirm whether growth is speeding up or slowing down. Valuation is fair on EV/EBITDA of 10.92x, supported by a trailing P/E of 14.68x inside the 10-18x utilities range and P/B of 1.81x for 12.5% ROE; I gave little weight to the cheap broad-market peer rank because it does not compare utilities, and I ignored the 348% dividend yield, the +59.7% target upside (which does not fit the roughly Rs 170 price implied by the market cap and EPS) and the -100% estimate revisions as likely data errors. The biggest risk is that net debt of Rs 15,747 cr (4.44x EBITDA) and a 0.9 current ratio leave little cushion if regulatory income, already down from Rs 1,249 cr to Rs 903 cr, keeps falling or pending tariff appeals go against the company, and the results due from the 5 November board meeting could quickly change this view.

fundamental.thesis: NLC India (NLCINDIA) is a Navratna PSU lignite miner and thermal power generator (~0.51 GW installed capacity) with a nascent renewable pipeline, operating under regulated and quasi-regulated tariff structures. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue accelerated to +23.3% YoY (₹4,717 cr vs ₹3,826 cr in Q1FY26), driven by a 25% YoY jump in power generation to 8,262 MU — a genuine volume pickup — but Q1FY27 PAT is not yet extracted from official PDFs, and a structural concern is visible: PBT grew only 9.76% vs revenue's 23.29%, and EBITDA margins have contracted from a FY25 peak of 42.6% to 36.0% in Q1FY27 as interest and depreciation from aggressive capex outpace operating gains; tariff realisation has also fallen sharply from ₹3.74/kWh (FY25) to ₹2.45/kWh (FY26), squeezing per-unit economics even as volumes rise. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive regulated utility (per sector card), the 9.88× multiple sits at the P10 peer percentile — a 58% discount to the broad-market median of 23.3× — and trailing P/E of 12.75× is at the low end of the 10–18× Utilities benchmark, making valuation clearly cheap; forward P/E of 11.99× marginally below trailing signals consensus expects modest earnings growth, though the single analyst covering this stock (target ₹390, +54%) provides very weak signal. The dominant risk to the thesis is further tariff compression from CERC regulatory resets combined with rising debt servicing on a capex-heavy balance sheet (D/E flagged as elevated by yfinance; FCF was ₹-2,779 cr in FY26), which could keep PAT margins structurally below FY25 levels even as revenue grows.

Aegis Logistics runs gas and liquid terminals, with gas at 92% of H1 FY27 revenue (₹4,205 cr, 20.3% margin) and the smaller liquid segment at 8% (₹366 cr, 63.0% margin); the Energy card's PSU and crude framing fits it poorly, so it is closer to a volume and tariff business. H1 FY27 revenue rose 13.9% YoY to ₹4,570 cr and PAT rose 106.4% to ₹865 cr, but the 'accelerating' signal mixes period lengths: Q2 figures derived from H1 minus Q1 show revenue slowing from +37.1% in Q1 to about -3.5% (about ₹2,213 cr), PAT growth slowing from +268.9% to about +32% (about ₹381 cr), and EBITDA margin falling from 31.9% to about 18.9%, while H1 cash conversion was only 0.19x CFO/PAT against 1.83x in FY26. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, 25.1× is about 8% above the broad-market median (P56) and trailing P/E of 39.3× is P57, so the grade is fair, but this is not a true peer comparison, and at 97.9% of the 52-week range with P/B of 5.95× on 15.3% ROE the upside looks limited. The biggest risk is that earnings quality is unproven, because PAT is not yet converting to cash, the table's roughly ₹1,553 cr trailing PAT does not reconcile with the roughly ₹900 cr implied by the P/E, and management guidance is unavailable; I also disregarded the 81% dividend yield and 47.24 debt/equity as likely data-format errors, and the consensus upside does not match the price implied by the 52-week range and market cap.

fundamental.thesis: Chennai Petroleum is a standalone refiner and IOC subsidiary, so its earnings track gross refining margins (GRM, the profit per barrel of crude processed) rather than administered retail fuel prices. Taking the official H1FY27 filing (₹51,414 cr revenue, ₹3,278 cr PAT) and subtracting Q1 gives an implied Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹22,055 cr, up roughly 10% YoY. That is a sharp slowdown from +57% in Q1, so the pre-computed 'accelerating' label is misleading because it mixes half-year and quarterly periods. Implied Q2 PAT was ₹2,247 cr, a 10.2% margin, driven by GRM rising to $8.78/bbl from $3.22 a year ago and a ₹385 cr one-off retrospective price adjustment, even though crude throughput fell 4.5%. On live ratios the stock looks cheap, using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-intensive refiner: trailing P/E 5.4x, EV/EBITDA 3.8x and P/B 1.5x against a 32% ROE, all bottom-percentile versus the market and below the 8–14x energy band. However, these are peak-cycle refining margins, and next-year EPS estimates were cut 11.6% in the last 30 days, so normalised earnings likely put it closer to fair. The bigger worry is earnings quality: H1 operating cash flow was only ₹25 cr against ₹3,278 cr of profit (0.01x), receivables jumped from ₹235 cr to ₹2,008 cr, cash fell to near zero after dividends, and the auditor flagged board-composition non-compliance.

Ramkrishna Forgings makes forged auto and industrial components, with subsidiaries in the USA and Mexico and a rail joint venture in India. H1 FY27 revenue rose 36.3% YoY to Rs 2,621 cr and PAT recovered to Rs 117 cr from Rs 2.2 cr, a low base hit by a Rs 42 cr receivables provision; subtracting Q1 from H1 implies Q2 revenue of about Rs 1,404 cr (+54.6% YoY, up from +19.8% in Q1), PAT of about Rs 70 cr, and EBITDA margin steady at about 18%, up from 14.6% in H1 FY26. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 20.0x sits at P42 of a broad-market peer set with no close forging peers, so I grade it fair, not cheap: the 148x trailing P/E looks stale because filings imply about Rs 202 cr of trailing PAT and about 53x, while the 27.7x forward P/E implies about Rs 387 cr of PAT versus a roughly Rs 280 cr annualised Q2 run-rate. The biggest risk is that earnings are not converting to cash, with H1 operating cash flow of Rs 41.5 cr against Rs 390 cr of capex (free cash flow of -Rs 349 cr), and conviction is capped because the snapshot's price signals conflict, the extracted net debt looks too low against Rs 118.7 cr of H1 finance costs, and no guidance or sector KPIs were available.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, with ₹33.2L cr of deposits, ₹33.2L cr of advances and 9,706 branches, and its asset quality is very clean: GNPA is 1.11%, down from 1.15% at FY26-end, net NPA is 0.37% and credit cost is 44 bps. On volume, Q2FY27 deposits grew +18.8% YoY and advances grew +16.3%, but profitability is moving the wrong way. Management calls the 3.32% NIM a cycle low, ROA has fallen from 1.9% in FY26 to 1.48% in H1FY27, and H1 PAT of ₹35,869 cr is down -10.2% YoY on revenue down -4.1%, a 14.3% PAT margin. The ₹1,950 cr Q2 PAT figure (+12.7%) looks like an extraction error, and 30-day and 90-day FY EPS estimates have both been cut 5.6%. Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, 1.98x book on a 13.8% TTM ROE (12.1% in H1) is fair in absolute terms, but it ranks P79 among bank peers on P/B even though P/E sits at the peer median of 16.8x. The stock is at 8.6% of its 52-week range, which helps the entry but does not make it cheap. The biggest risk is an abrupt leadership change: a new MD/CEO effective immediately and the Deputy MD retiring by December. This comes with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 100%, LCR tight at 113%, and a 25 bps October rate hike that management expects to reprice the 70% floating book upward, which conflicts with the sector card's easing-cycle prior.

NTPC is India's largest power generator and earns mainly a regulated return on the plants it commissions, with a fast-growing solar business on top. The reported +19.9% H1 FY27 revenue growth is overstated because it compares ₹100,262 cr of total revenue with ₹83,660 cr of capacity and energy charges only; like-for-like growth is +9.65%, up from -0.4% in FY26 and +7.0% in Q1 FY27 (₹51,142 cr), with capacity charges, the core regulated earnings driver, up 6.73%, but Q2 FY27 standalone quarter figures and H1 PAT were not extracted, so the latest profit data is Q1 FY27 PAT of ₹6,896 cr (+12.9%), and the 'expanding' margin signals are unreliable because they mix quarterly, year-to-date and full-year periods. Using EV/EBITDA with P/B and ROE as the yardstick, the stock looks cheap against peers at 8.36x EV/EBITDA (sector median 11.6x), 11.9x trailing P/E (median 14.7x, static sector range 10-18x) and 1.73x book on 13.7% ROE, though the Adani names inflate those medians, POWERGRID and GAIL are comparably cheap, forward P/E of 12.81x sits above trailing even as FY EPS estimates rose 2.6% in 30 days, and the 314% dividend yield is a data error (probably about 3.14%), while the +30.6% consensus upside looks overstated because market cap and 52-week position imply a price near ₹361, or about +17% to the ₹423 target. The biggest risk is that final CERC orders under the 2024 tariff regulations are still pending, so capacity charges are billed provisionally and reported earnings, already complicated by regulatory deferral and deferred tax items, could be adjusted retrospectively.

fundamental.thesis: Shriram Finance is one of India's largest retail NBFCs, mainly lending against commercial vehicles, and it now has a 20% strategic shareholder in MUFG Bank, which put in ₹39,618 cr of fresh equity. In Q2 FY27 (H1 minus Q1 from the filings), revenue was about ₹13,774 cr, up 15.6% YoY, and PAT was ₹3,684 cr, up 59.1% YoY. Revenue growth has eased from +19.1% to about +16% while PAT margin widened from 19.0% to 26.7%, partly because the MUFG equity lowers borrowing needs, so the PAT jump overstates the gain in underlying loan economics (loan growth is ~15%). Valuation is graded on P/B plus ROE, the lender yardstick: P/B of 2.56x against ROE of 16.4% (diluted by the new capital) is fair rather than cheap, with P/B at P33 and trailing P/E of 16.8x at P44 among credit-services peers, and forward P/E of 12.9x plus +3.7% upward EPS revisions support the earnings path. The main watch-point is asset quality: gross NPA has crept up from 4.54% to 4.65% standalone and impairment charges rose 27.5% against roughly 15% loan growth, even though net NPA and provision coverage are improving.

fundamental.thesis: Canara Bank is a large public sector bank (62.93% GoI ownership) and one of India's top-5 lenders by advances (₹13.6L cr), with a franchise spanning retail, wholesale, and treasury segments; the key yardstick here is P/B vs ROE, per the sector card, not P/E. H1FY27 shows a notable bifurcation: PAT grew strongly +31.3% YoY to ₹10,562 cr on dramatically improved asset quality (Gross NPA 1.33%, Net NPA 0.30%, PCR 95.34%), but total income contracted -3.38% YoY — revenue trajectory has decelerated from +7.7% (FY26) to -3.4% (H1FY27), driven by treasury revenue declining -18% YoY and NIM compression (2.06% FY26 vs 2.51% in Q4FY26), while PAT margin has expanded from 11.7% (FY26) to 13.1% (H1FY27) on sharply lower credit costs. At P/B of 1.02× against ROE of 15.9%, the stock is unambiguously cheap by the sector card's prescribed lender yardstick — sector card benchmark is P/B < 1.5 with ROE > 12% = cheap — and sits at P0 (cheapest) in its 14-peer regional bank cohort on both trailing P/E (6.1×, -64% vs median 16.8×) and forward P/E (5.7×), though much of this structural discount is explained by PSU overhang and below-median CASA (29.86% vs private sector ~40%+). The single biggest risk is NIM pressure persisting through the deposit repricing cycle — NIM at 2.06% for FY26 is already thin for a PSU bank and any further compression from EBLR-linked loan repricing faster than deposit cost decline would erode the PAT margin expansion thesis and keep revenue growth negative.

Shree Cement is a major Indian cement producer outside the UltraTech-Adani duo, with about 69 MT of capacity reported at Q4 FY26 and a growing premium mix (28.7% vs 21.1% a year ago). Q2 FY27 revenue growth accelerated to +23.9% YoY at Rs 5,897 cr from +18.0% in Q1 on 14% volume growth, but PAT fell 15.2% to Rs 263 cr, its third straight YoY decline, as EBITDA margin dropped from 23.8% to 17.2% QoQ and EBITDA per tonne fell 8% YoY to Rs 966, still inside the Rs 900-1,100 healthy range. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick alongside EBITDA per tonne, the stock grades expensive but with lower confidence: the snapshot's 30.4x is 70% above the 17.9x peer median, though filing numbers suggest a figure nearer 18x, so that multiple looks unreliable, while the 48.6x trailing P/E (P80, 37.3x median) on falling profits and a position near the 52-week low (19% of range) still leave little valuation comfort. The biggest risk is that fuel costs keep margins under pressure with crude rising, as FY27 EPS estimates have already been cut 14.8% in 30 days and the 33.2x forward P/E still assumes a profit recovery.

fundamental.thesis: IndusInd Bank is a mid-sized private lender, heavy on vehicle finance (28% of loans, 58% retail), that is still rebuilding after the FY26 accounting-discrepancy year in which full-year PAT fell 65% to ₹891 cr and ROA dropped to 0.17%. Per the H1FY27 filing, total income rose 26.8% YoY to ₹23,873 cr and PAT rose 36.4% to ₹2,279 cr, but this flatters the core business: the comparison base includes a Q2FY26 loss, Q1FY27 includes a one-off ₹868 cr IFR transfer, and operating profit actually fell 7.9% YoY to ₹10,323 cr. Loan growth has recovered from -8.5% (FY26) to +11% YoY, but NIM has slipped to 3.23% from 3.39–3.48%, credit cost is elevated at 1.4%, cost-to-income is high at 57.9%, and annualised Q2 ROE is only 7.4%. Using the bank yardstick (P/B with ROE, ignoring the distorted 80× trailing P/E), a P/B of 1.08× (P29 vs peers, 26% below the 1.5× median) fits sub-par returns of about 7% ROE, so the valuation is fair rather than cheap; the cheap case only holds if ROE recovers toward 12%+. The biggest risk is that the earnings recovery stalls as NIM compression and above-normal vehicle and microfinance credit costs hold ROA under 1%.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Life Insurance is India's second-largest private life insurer with a 10.9% individual WRP market share, distributing through a 59% bancassurance channel anchored by parent HDFC Bank across ULIPs (43% of mix), participating (27%), and a rapidly-growing protection segment. H1FY27 gross premium income accelerated to +16.2% YoY (₹39,734 cr) and PAT grew +13.7% to ₹1,133 cr — a clear improvement from FY26's +5.6% PAT growth — driven by retail protection (+42% YoY) and renewal premium growth (+15%), though embedded value VNB growth in 9MFY26 lagged at only +7% as VNB margin compressed to 24.4% from 25.1% prior year. The sector card prescribes P/EV as the primary yardstick for life insurers, but the extracted embedded value figure (₹615 cr) is implausibly low against a ₹1.2L cr market cap and cannot be reliably used; on peer-relative forward P/E (46x, P50 in the Insurance – Life peer set), HDFCLIFE is fairly valued, though P/B of 6.85x against ROE of only 11.3% is stretched, and the stock's position at 11% of its 52-week range offers a modestly improved entry. The single biggest risk is the combination of rising expenses-of-management ratio (21.2% in FY26 to 22.2% in H1FY27) and declining VNB margin, which signals new business profitability erosion that may constrain embedded value compounding even as top-line premiums accelerate.

SBI Life is a listed Indian life insurer with a market cap of about Rs 1.8 lakh crore and is also taking over the Sahara India Life book under an IRDAI direction. Q2 FY27 results were filed on 27 Oct, but no revenue or PAT was extracted, so the last usable growth figures are Q1 FY27 revenue +16.9% and PAT +21.9%; revenue growth has been range-bound at +16% to +19% rather than clearly slowing as flagged, while the 'expanding' margin signal is unreliable because the table mixes periods and rupee scales, and H1 FY27 new business value of Rs 3,270 cr has no comparable base because the H1 FY26 KPI appears mis-scaled. Using P/EV, the right yardstick for a life insurer, the stock trades at about 2.1x (Rs 1.8 lakh crore market cap vs Rs 87,350 cr embedded value), which I grade fair with low confidence because no peer or historical P/EV was provided; the 71.7x trailing P/E (peer median 53.7x) and 9.3x P/B (peer median 6.8x) look expensive but are poor measures for this business, while the 15% dividend yield looks wrong and the price implied by the 52-week position (about Rs 1,782) conflicts with the one implied by the consensus target upside (about Rs 1,658). The biggest risk is that the core franchise is weakening while the market still expects growth: 13-month persistency is 84.35% vs 87.11% in H1 FY26, the expense ratio has risen from 10.9% to 12.05% across those reported periods, and EPS estimates are drifting down (next-FY -1.6% over 90 days) despite 34 of 35 analysts rating it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Adani Green is India's largest renewable power producer (20,763 MW operational, up 24% YoY, plus the largest battery-storage installation in the country at Khavda), and it earns money by adding capacity and selling power under 25-year fixed-tariff contracts. At 31.8× against a utilities peer median of 11.6× (P100 in sector), and P/B of 12.7× on an ROE of only 7.6%, the stock is clearly expensive. fundamental.thesis: Indian Hotels (IHCL) runs India's largest hotel chain, with Taj and other brands across 670 hotels including 280 in the pipeline. It earns more and more from asset-light management fees, which grew 25% YoY in Q2, and it is still early in a RevPAR (revenue per available room) upcycle, up 25% YoY in Q2 and 28% for full-service hotels. Q2FY27 revenue rose 21.0% YoY to ₹2,566 cr, up from +14.6% in Q1FY27. PAT rose 23.0% to ₹349 cr. Management raised full-year revenue guidance from 12-14% to 15-17%, and H1 cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 1.27x, FCF ₹546 cr). The 'contracting' margin signal mostly reflects comparing a seasonally weak Q2 against full-year figures: on a same-quarter basis the EBITDA margin (30.7%) and PAT margin (13.6%) are roughly flat to slightly up YoY. On valuation, hotels are capital-intensive, so I used EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick. At 28.2x, IHCL sits around the 61st percentile of its sector, with a trailing P/E of 44.5x (P59) and a forward P/E of 35.6x. That is fair, not cheap, for 20%+ earnings growth, and the stock sits at 38.5% of its 52-week range. Note that the snapshot's 49% dividend yield and 18.99 debt/equity look like data-unit errors, given ₹4,369 cr of gross cash. The biggest risk is that a premium-multiple discretionary stock gets de-rated in a risk-off market with crude above $100, which could squeeze travel and MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences and events) demand even while operating numbers stay strong.

Berger Paints is a listed decorative and industrial paint maker, a consumer-style franchise whose margins and market share are under structural pressure from Birla Opus's entry. Q1 FY27 revenue rose 12.0% YoY to Rs 3,584 cr and PAT rose 28.6% to Rs 405 cr, with reported revenue growth improving from +0.4% in Q3 FY26 to +6.7% in Q4 FY26 and +12.0% in Q1 FY27, and Q1 volume growth (8.4%) ahead of price growth (5%); however, the trend is less clean than the signals suggest because the table mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods and possibly standalone and consolidated figures, PAT growth outpaced EBITDA growth of 15.0%, and Q2 guidance implies price growth of 7.5-8.5% matching or exceeding volume growth of 7.5-8%. Using the paint-franchise P/E yardstick from the sector card, the 50.9x trailing P/E is inside the 30-60x norm and the stock is mid-range at 47.8% of its 52-week range, so I grade it fair; its P87 rank against Materials peers is inflated by cyclical metal and cement names, and it remains cheaper than direct franchise peers ASIANPAINT and PIDILITIND. The biggest risk is that crude at $104 and rising squeezes gross margins while competition limits further price increases, with Q2 results due on 5 Nov 2026 as the near-term test of management's 15-17% operating margin guidance.

fundamental.thesis: Polycab is India's largest wires and cables maker, with about 30-31% share of the organised market. It is scaling a consumer electricals (FMEG) business and a smaller EPC arm, and has net cash of ₹4,520cr and an 11-day working-capital cycle. Revenue growth sped up from +39% YoY in Q1 FY27 to +53% in Q2 FY27 (₹9,900cr), and PAT rose 43% to ₹990cr. PAT margin edged up to 10.0% from 9.4% in FY26. FMEG grew 124% and posted its first double-digit EBIT margin (10.1%). Much of the headline growth is copper price pass-through, though: copper rose 40-45% in H1, while wire volumes grew only 10.5% and cable volumes about 5%. Underlying demand is healthy but well below the +53% headline. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, which suits this capital-intensive business. At 35.0x it sits close to the sector peer median of 34.0x (P53). Trailing P/E is 53.8x (P50) and forward P/E is 38.5x, which points to expected earnings growth. On the sector card's 50-80x range for electricals this is fair, not cheap, and the stock is at 99.8% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that copper-inflated revenue and record margins revert as commodity prices normalise or UltraTech's entry into wires squeezes pricing. That risk is larger because, in a risk-off market, a stock priced for perfection can lose 30-50% of its valuation multiple quickly.

On the lender yardstick (price-to-book plus ROE), the stock trades at 0.74x book against a 12-15% ROE, the cheapest in its 15-bank peer set on P/B (P0) and about 50% below the 1.5x median, which grades as cheap. fundamental.thesis: IGIL is India's listed entity of the International Gemological Institute — a global leader in diamond and gemstone grading services with an asset-light, high-margin business model riding the lab-grown diamond (LGD) certification wave across 16 global subsidiaries. Q1FY27 revenue grew +23.2% YoY to ₹371 cr, with PAT growing faster at +31% YoY to ₹166 cr and PAT margin expanding to 44.7% — PAT consistently outpacing revenue is a quality signal of operating leverage, and EBITDA margin recovered to 64.3% in Q1FY27 after holding at 60-61% in FY26; revenue growth has re-accelerated modestly from the steady +17–18% corridor. Trailing P/E of 30× sits at P41 in the broad market (14.6% below the median of 35.2×) and EV/EBITDA of 20.87× is also below peer median — fair to leaning cheap for a 64%-EBITDA-margin business growing at 23%, and the forward P/E of 20.28× (a meaningful discount to trailing) confirms consensus expects earnings acceleration to continue. The single biggest risk to this thesis is the reported debt/equity of 9.59 — likely legacy acquisition financing from the PE-backed IPO structure — which, combined with structural LGD average-realized-price deflation (-3% YoY in 2025), could squeeze cash flows and de-rate the multiple sharply if certification volume growth disappoints.

JSW Infrastructure runs ports with about 186 MTPA of capacity, targeting 400 MTPA by 2030, and is building a fast-growing rail and logistics arm. Q2FY27 revenue grew 17.0% YoY to ₹1,481 cr, extending a slow slowdown from +20.2% to +18.1% to +17.0% over recent periods. PAT fell 11.1% YoY to ₹328 cr, a deeper drop than Q1's -8.2%, as finance costs rose about 125% and the PAT margin shrank from about 29-31% in FY26 to 22.1%; cargo volume growth was only 4% for H1, while logistics revenue grew about 71%. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy port business, the stock trades at 25.6x, around P58 of the peer set, and its 42.2x trailing P/E sits inside the 28-45x Industrials band, so it is fairly valued. Forward P/E of 27x already assumes a strong earnings rebound, while consensus estimates are being trimmed slightly (-0.4% for FY, -1.8% for next FY). The main risk is that heavy capex and acquisitions keep pushing up interest costs and free cash flow stays negative (₹-384 cr in H1), so earnings per share keep falling, made worse by dilution from the ₹6,555 cr QIP.

fundamental.thesis: PTC Industries is a specialty investment-casting manufacturer supplying precision components to aerospace, defence, and energy sectors, having scaled consolidated revenue from ₹308cr (FY25) to ₹603cr (FY26, +95.7% YoY) on India's defence indigenisation and PLI tailwinds. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial, PTCIL trades at 203× EV/EBITDA (sector median 28–45×) and 259× trailing P/E, ranking at P100 (most expensive) among 473 market peers, while a P/B of 18.4× against a 7% ROE and Debt/Equity of 17.34× signals extreme valuation risk with no earnings support. Sustained EPS estimate cuts (-13.1% over 90 days, -14.6% on next-FY) while sell-side ratings stay uniformly bullish is a textbook pre-derating pattern, and any further slip in the defence order pipeline or margin recovery could catalyse a 30–50% de-rating — the historical norm for industrial cycle disappointments.

fundamental.thesis: RHI Magnesita India is one of India's leading refractories manufacturers, supplying high-temperature resistant materials primarily to steel, cement, and glass industries; it sits within the RHI Magnesita global group and commands meaningful market share in domestic installed capacity. Q1FY27 revenue grew 5.6% YoY to ₹1,014 cr — decelerating from a peak of +14.3% in H1FY26 — while PAT surged 83.2% YoY to ₹65 cr on a low base; more importantly, EBITDA margins expanded to 14.5% (vs 10.8% a year ago), recovering toward FY25 levels of 13.6% and signalling genuine operational improvement after FY26 was distorted by a ₹556 cr goodwill impairment on the RHIMIRL subsidiary. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for this capital-intensive business, the stock trades at 17.82× vs a broad-market peer median of 23.3× (P34 rank), which the system flags as fairly valued — not cheap enough to compensate for the elevated risk profile given the impairment history and debt load. The single biggest risk is the extreme financial leverage (D/E of 12.6) which, combined with revenue growth decelerating to low single digits and a brand-new MD/CEO at the helm, leaves the business highly exposed if steel/cement end-market demand softens.

fundamental.thesis: RVNL is a Navratna PSU that executes Indian Railways' capital works (new lines, gauge conversion, electrification), giving it captive but government-budget-dependent revenue and making order execution pace — not demand — the binding constraint on earnings. Using EV/EBITDA per the Sector Card — the correct yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials — RVNL trades at 70.3× versus a broad-market peer median of 23.3× (P95 of universe, +201% premium), with trailing P/E of 58.95× also exceeding the sector upper bound of 45× and P/B of 5.24× on just 9% ROE flagging value trap risk; no order book data is available in this pack to justify a supercycle premium, so the stock is graded expensive. EV/EBITDA of 35.23× — the preferred metric for this capital-intensive business per the sector card — places SCI in the upper-mid of the Industrials range (28–45×) and at P74 vs broad-market peers, indicating FAIR valuation; the trailing P/E of 10.65× superficially flatters cheapness (P7 vs peers), but the forward P/E of 93.71× (P99 vs peers) explicitly prices in a dramatic earnings collapse, making the trailing read unreliable as a through-cycle signal. The single biggest risk is a cyclical mean-reversion in global shipping freight rates compressing earnings from currently elevated levels, amplified by an unresolved six-year government disinvestment process, going-concern uncertainties across three Middle East joint ventures, and high leverage (D/E 29.45) that leaves limited cushion if rates deteriorate.

Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-intensive cement business, 9.7× is above the 5–8× mid-cycle range for cyclicals, while the trailing P/E of 12.4× sits at the bottom edge of the 12–22× Materials band. P/B of 1.15× and a price near its 52-week low look cheap, but forward P/E (12.8×) is above trailing and FY EPS estimates have been cut 41% over 90 days, so I grade it fair, not cheap: falling earnings are eating the apparent discount. fundamental.thesis: CCL Products is one of the world's largest private-label instant coffee makers, with plants in India and Vietnam (Ngon Coffee, which earned ₹53 cr PAT in Q2 alone), plus a small but growing branded domestic business; it trades as FMCG but is mostly a B2B coffee processor exposed to green-coffee price swings. Revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +44.5% (H1FY26) and +38.5% (Q3FY26) to +13.7% in Q1FY27 and +10.5% for H1FY27 (₹2,411 cr). That implies Q2FY27 grew only about +7–8% (≈₹1,211 cr vs ≈₹1,127 cr), most likely as coffee-price pass-through fades. Profits are still growing much faster than sales: H1 PAT is up 42.5% to ₹247 cr, PAT margin has widened from 8.0% to 10.2%, and cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 1.78x, FCF ₹414 cr). Valuation is fair rather than cheap. I used EV/EBITDA because this is a capital- and working-capital-heavy processor, not a classic staples brand: EV/EBITDA is 21.6x (P46 vs market) and trailing P/E is 38.9x, at the bottom of the FMCG 40–60x band but rich for a commodity-linked exporter. Forward P/E of 24.1x already prices in strong earnings growth, and the stock sits at 77% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps slowing toward single digits as coffee prices normalise, while margin gains, which drove most of this year's profit growth, become harder to repeat.

Emami is a mid-sized Indian personal-care and OTC/healthcare FMCG company (Navratna, BoroPlus, Zandu, Kesh King) with strong niche brands, and it has just completed a buyback that extinguished 73 lakh shares. The latest reliable numbers from official filings show FY26 revenue of about ₹3,780 cr, down 0.8% YoY, and PAT of ₹775 cr, down 3.4%, with a 20.5% PAT margin. Quarterly growth has been choppy and has not shown a clear trend: Q3FY26 grew 9.8% while H1FY26 fell 5.2%. EBITDA margin has eased from the Q3 peak of 38.9% to 27.7% for the year, while gross margin held steady at around 70%. Q1FY27 extraction is missing, the Q2 FY26 row is clearly corrupt and is ignored, and Q2 FY27 results are not yet in the data. Using the P/E yardstick the FMCG card prescribes, trailing P/E of 22.5x (forward 18.5x, EV/EBITDA 17.7x) sits well below the sector's normal 40-65x band, so the stock grades cheap, and it trades near its 52-week low. However, the sector card warns that cheap FMCG usually signals a structural growth problem, and flat revenue with high ad spend (19.6% of revenue) fits that pattern. The biggest risk is that the core domestic business keeps stalling on volumes while sell-side earnings estimates are still being cut (-5.2% over 90 days), which would turn the low multiple into a value trap rather than a re-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Godfrey Phillips India is India's second-largest cigarette maker (Philip Morris-affiliated) with a growing FMCG business, commanding a dominant position in the premium cigarette segment. Q1FY27 revenue surged 110.6% YoY to ₹3,820 cr — likely reflecting inclusion of low-margin tobacco leaf trading — but PAT collapsed 44.3% YoY to ₹198 cr as PAT margin compressed sharply from 19.7% to 5.2%, a severe quality-of-earnings deterioration that makes the revenue acceleration misleading. At trailing P/E of 23.2×, the stock trades at a 34% discount to the broad market median and well below the FMCG sector norm of 40–65×, placing it in the 'cheap' band by sector yardstick — however, tobacco names structurally attract a regulatory/ESG discount globally, and if the underlying PAT margin has genuinely structurally compressed (FY26 CFO/PAT only 0.34×), the apparent cheapness may be a value trap. fundamental.thesis: Patanjali Foods is India's largest edible oils company (formerly Ruchi Soya), with a fast-growing FMCG overlay spanning biscuits, nutrition, and home/personal care under the Patanjali brand — but edible oils still account for roughly 70%+ of revenues, making this a commodity-FMCG hybrid rather than a pure compounder, and that matters critically for how to frame the valuation. Q1FY27 delivered record revenue of ₹11,337 cr (+29.3% YoY, accelerating from +20.9% in Q2FY26) and PAT of ₹336 cr (+86.1% YoY), but underlying quality is deteriorating: gross margin compressed from 15.26% (Q2FY26) to 13.42% (Q1FY27), EBITDA margin fell from 6.2% to 4.8%, and PAT margin contracted to 3.0% — a persistent multi-quarter contraction signal that runs counter to the top-line acceleration. At trailing P/E 25.43×, the stock screens cheap versus the FMCG sector benchmark of 40–60×, but the discount is structurally warranted by the commodity-heavy business mix; EV/EBITDA of 25× (P55 vs broad-market peers) and P/E peer rank of P32 both point to fair value rather than genuine mispricing, and the sector card's own caution — 'cheap FMCG usually means a structural problem' — applies directly here. The overriding risk is extreme balance sheet leverage (D/E 21.3×) combined with negative FCF (CFO/PAT −1.13× in Q2FY26) — at a 5.29% US 10Y yield and with PAT margins at 3%, any commodity cost spike or interest burden increase could rapidly destroy earnings entirely.

Radico Khaitan is one of India's largest spirits makers, known for premium brands like Magic Moments and Rampur, and benefits from the premiumisation trend in alcohol. Q2FY27 gross revenue was about ₹5,583 cr, up 10.4% YoY, but growth has slowed from +29.4% in Q2FY26 and +24.7% in FY26 to +10.4% in each of the last two periods, while PAT jumped roughly 66% YoY to about ₹232 cr (H1 PAT ₹462 cr, +71%) as margins expanded and net debt fell to ₹175 cr. On the FMCG yardstick of trailing P/E (sector card norm 40–65×), the stock is expensive at 81.8× trailing P/E and 40.3× EV/EBITDA, sits at about 96% of its 52-week range, and ranks around P89–P93 against the broad market; the 51× forward P/E and sell-side EPS upgrades of +19% over 90 days support earnings momentum but leave little room for a miss. The biggest risk is a de-rating if revenue growth keeps slowing toward single digits while the price already assumes continued strong profit growth, and a 'Change in Management' filing on 2026-10-27 has not yet been assessed.

fundamental.thesis: Zydus Wellness is a mid-cap consumer-wellness company (Glucon-D, Complan, Sugar Free, Nutralite, Everyuth). It is now growing mostly through acquisitions: the Naturell consolidation and the GBP 239 million Comfort Click (UK) buy. The extracted filings show FY26 revenue of ₹396 cr (+46.2% YoY) but PAT down 43.2% to ₹20 cr, with EBITDA margin falling from 18.4% (Q1 FY26) to 12.0% and finance costs up 718%. These figures are not internally consistent, though. FY25 is shown at ₹2,709 cr against FY26 at ₹396 cr, which looks like standalone and consolidated numbers mixed together, and the extracted results stop at FY26, so the trend should be treated as directional only. On the FMCG P/E yardstick from the sector card, trailing P/E of 81.7x sits well above the 40–65x sector norm. EV/EBITDA of 38.5x is at P80 against peers and ROE is only 3.4%, so I grade it expensive. Forward P/E of 28.9x does price in a sharp earnings recovery, but sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 6–7% over 90 days, which undercuts that recovery case. The biggest risk is the acquisition-funded leverage (net debt/EBITDA 6.47x on the filed figures) meeting slower integration. Q2 results on 3 Nov are the next real data point, so conviction stays low until then.

Cyient is a mid-cap engineering-services firm with three businesses: design and engineering services (DET, about 74% of revenue), electronics contract manufacturing (DLM), and a loss-making semiconductor unit, and it recently bought TAO Digital for about ₹2,156 cr. H1 FY27 revenue grew 23.4% YoY to ₹4,311 cr, but that growth is largely acquisition-driven, and PAT fell 19.7% YoY to ₹241 cr, so the PAT margin dropped from 8.6% to 5.6%. Profit has now fallen in every reported period (-24.9% in Q3FY26, -32.3% in Q1FY27, -19.7% in H1FY27), and the semiconductor unit lost ₹58 cr at a -16.5% margin. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA together, and the stock looks fair rather than cheap: trailing P/E of 22.6x sits at the bottom of the 22–30x IT range, and EV/EBITDA of 11.4x ranks P16 against the broad market, but ROE is only 7.8%. The low 11.9x forward P/E rests on analyst estimates that were cut 18% over the last 90 days, so it should not be trusted yet. The biggest risk is that semiconductor losses and integrating TAO keep eating into the steady DET profits, and the data has gaps: the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹1,498 cr conflicts with the filings, Q1FY27 shows two different growth rates, and the reported debt/equity and dividend-yield figures look like data errors.
